sub: Named after “the chargers” (al-ʿādiyāt), its opening word
theme: Swearing by charging war-horses, the surah says man is ungrateful to his Lord and fiercely attached to wealth, then warns that the graves will be emptied and what hides in hearts exposed.
story: Reports differ on whether it came in Makkah or Madinah; its style fits the earliest Makkan period. Arabia was full of tribal raids then, and no one slept safely for fear of an attack at dawn.

Reportedly, the Prophet ﷺ sent a cavalry unit to a clan of Banū Kinānah, and no news came back. The hypocrites said its men had been killed. The surah came down to tell him they were safe and had raided the enemy.
The oath is either by war-horses charging in Allah’s path or by camels running in Hajj. A horse gives everything for the master who feeds it; man, given everything by his Lord, is still ungrateful.

sections.title: By the horses charging at dawn
sections.meaning: Allah swears by war-horses at full gallop: panting as they run, striking sparks from the rocks with their hooves, raiding at dawn, raising clouds of dust, and plunging together into the middle of the enemy.
points: Raising dust, then plunging into the enemy’s midst
sections.matters: The oath sets up the charge that follows. A horse, fed by its master with food he did not create, risks its life for him. Man, given everything by his Lord, does not even thank Him.
sections.story: Reportedly, the Prophet ﷺ sent a cavalry unit and heard nothing back. Hypocrites claimed it had been wiped out. The surah came to reassure him that it was safe and had raided the people it was sent to.
explained: Wal-ʿādiyāti ḍabḥā: by the chargers, panting. Ḍabḥ is the sound from a horse’s chest as it runs hard. Their hooves strike the rocks and throw sparks (qadḥā). They raid at dawn (ṣubḥā), the time Arabs attacked, because a raid in the dark was seen as cowardly.

They stir up dust clouds (naqʿā) that only a hard charge makes at that hour, then burst together into the middle of the enemy (jamʿā) without fear. In the other view, these are camels in Hajj, running from ʿArafah to Muzdalifah and on to Minā.
teaches: Allah swears by His creation to stress a truth; people swear only by Allah.
An animal repays a little care with loyalty; man owes his Lord far more.
Look at the loyalty around you and ask how loyal you are to Allah.
sections.hook: Five short ayat ending ḍabḥā, qadḥā, ṣubḥā, naqʿā, jamʿā. They move in order: run, spark, raid, dust, break in. Ayah 6 starts page 600.

sections.title: Man is ungrateful to his Lord
sections.meaning: This is what the oath is about: man is kanūd, ungrateful to his Lord. He is a witness to it himself, or Allah is witness to it. And his love of wealth is intense.
points: Man is ungrateful to his Lord
And he is witness to that
And he is fierce in his love of wealth
sections.matters: The heart of the surah. It names two faults, ingratitude and love of wealth, and they feed each other: love of wealth is what makes a person hold back what he owes his Lord.
sections.story: Reportedly ayah 6 was revealed about al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah. Its words are general, though: most people carry these faults, except those Allah guides.
explained: Kanūd: the ungrateful one, who counts his troubles and forgets the favours, or who holds back what he owes his Lord. It shows in his own words and deeds, so he is witness against himself; or Allah is the witness, which is a serious warning.

Al-khayr here means wealth. His love for it is shadīd: intense, or it makes him stingy. Earning and saving wealth is not blamed; love of it filling the heart until duties are forgotten is. Water under a boat carries it, but water inside it sinks it.
teaches: Count your blessings, not only your troubles.
Your deeds show whether you are grateful.
Earn wealth, but keep it out of your heart.
Love of wealth is what makes people hold back what they owe.
sections.hook: Each ayah ends la- plus a rhyme: la-kanūd, la-shahīd, la-shadīd. Ayat 7 and 8 both open wa innahu (“and indeed he”).

sections.title: Graves emptied, hearts laid bare
sections.meaning: Does he not know? When the graves are overturned and what is in the hearts is brought out, their Lord on that Day is fully aware of them, and repays them.
points: Doesn’t he know? The graves will be overturned
What is in the chests will be exposed
That Day their Lord is fully aware of them
sections.matters: This is the cure for both faults. Whoever remembers that his hidden intentions and motives will be brought out will not stay ungrateful or let wealth rule him.
sections.story: No specific incident. It turns the man described above toward the Hereafter he has forgotten.
explained: Afalā yaʿlam: does this deceived man not know? The dead will be brought out of their graves for the gathering, and ḥuṣṣila mā fī aṣ-ṣudūr: what hid in the chests, faith or disbelief, good or evil, will be sorted and shown. The secret becomes public.

Allah always knows His servants. Ayah 11 ties His full awareness to that Day because that is when He repays them for what He knows, the seen and the hidden. Nothing is missed, and no one is wronged in the slightest.
teaches: Intentions are judged, not only actions.
What you hide today will be public on that Day.
Remembering the grave cures greed and ingratitude.
sections.hook: The section starts at the ۞ mark on page 600, with ayah 9. Ayat 9 and 10 rhyme: al-qubūr, aṣ-ṣudūr. Ayah 11 ends la-khabīr, like section 2’s la- endings.

groups.text: By the horses racing and panting, striking sparks with their hooves.
Raiding at dawn, raising dust, and plunging together into the middle of the enemy.
Man is ungrateful to his Lord, and he himself is witness to it.
Doesn’t he know? When graves are emptied and hearts exposed, their Lord knows them fully that Day.

1.explain: Al-ʿādiyāt ḍabḥā: the chargers, panting, the sound from a horse’s chest at full gallop. Either war-horses in Allah’s path, or camels running in Hajj.
1.why: Reportedly, the Prophet ﷺ sent a unit under al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr to a clan of Banū Kinānah, and no news came. The hypocrites said they were killed. The surah came to say they were safe and had raided.

2.explain: Al-mūriyāti qadḥā: striking sparks as their hooves hit the rocks. Other views: the riders lighting their fires at night, or men stirring up war.

3.explain: Al-mughīrāti ṣubḥā: raiding at dawn. The Prophet ﷺ would wait at dawn: if he heard the adhan from a people, he left them alone.

4.explain: Atharna bihi naqʿā: they stir up dust at the place of the charge, the kind of dust cloud only a hard, fast run raises at dawn.

5.explain: Wasaṭna bihi jamʿā: they burst together into the middle of the enemy host, without the least fear.

6.explain: The point of the oath. Kanūd: ungrateful, the one who counts his troubles and forgets Allah’s favours, or who holds back what he owes his Lord.
6.why: Reportedly revealed about al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah.

7.explain: He is a witness to his own ingratitude: it shows in his words and deeds. Or Allah is witness to it, which is a serious warning.

8.explain: Al-khayr here means wealth. He loves it intensely, or his love of it makes him stingy. Earning wealth is allowed; letting it rule the heart is the fault.

9.explain: Afalā yaʿlam: doesn’t he know? Buʿthira: the graves are overturned and the dead brought out to be gathered. The ۞ mark falls on this ayah.

10.explain: Ḥuṣṣila: what hid in the chests (faith or disbelief, good or evil) is sorted out and brought into the open. The secret becomes public.

11.explain: Khabīr: fully aware. Allah always knows, but that Day is named because it is when He repays them for everything, with no injustice.
